title: The provider
hook: in Persian again: He is the one who gives daily bread (Jaap)

segments.voice: Yesterday, husnal charaag, the lamp of beauty, and your line, makes a room golden. Today the Persian lines keep going, and come down to the kitchen table.

Pick up a slice of bread and count the hands. Someone plowed a field and planted the wheat, then watched the sky all summer hoping for rain. A harvester driver, a miller, a trucker on a night highway, a baker up at four, a cashier, whoever carried the bag home. One slice, and dozens of people you'll never meet. Behind them, the rain and the sun and the soil, which nobody made. Every meal is a long chain of giving, and Jaap Sahib names the start of it.
screen: `ONE SLICE OF BREAD.` → `DOZENS OF HANDS.` → `A LONG CHAIN OF GIVING.`

segments.voice: In its Persian lines, Jaap says the One is rozi dihind, the giver of daily bread, and raazak, the provider. Rozi comes from roz, a day: the day's portion, the food, the wages, the livelihood that keeps a household going until tomorrow. Punjabi still says rozi roti for earning a living, the daily bread and the daily flatbread. Raazak is an Arabic word for the One who provides for every creature. So in the middle of all the cosmic praise, timeless, formless, sun of suns, Jaap stops at something as plain as lunch. That's very Sikh. Guru Nanak, in Japji, says there is one Giver for all living beings, and asks never to forget that One. But notice the Sikh balance. Trusting the Provider has never meant sitting and waiting. The three pillars Sikhs are taught are naam japna, remembering the Name; kirat karni, honest work; and vand chhakna, sharing what you have. You earn your bread honestly, thank the Giver for it, and share it. That's why every gurdwara has a langar, a free kitchen where anyone can eat. The bread passes through Sikh hands and goes straight back out to whoever walks in the door. In Sikh practice, the chain of giving doesn't end at your plate; it runs through it.
screen: `ROZI: THE DAY'S PORTION.` · `RAAZAK: THE ONE WHO PROVIDES.` · `ONE GIVER FOR ALL BEINGS.` · `EARN, THANK, SHARE: THE LANGAR.` · then, large: `DAILY BREAD.`

segments.voice: Hold something you're about to eat, or think of the last thing you ate, and trace it back one pair of hands at a time: who sold it, who carried it, who made it, who grew it, thanking each one silently. Then go one step further, to the rain, the sun and the soil, and rest there with your breath. If you pray, you can thank the Giver of daily bread.
The provider. Rozi dihind, raazak: in Jaap's Persian lines, the One who gives every creature its daily bread.
Your line: daily bread. It comes in, and some of it goes on to someone else. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs are taught to earn honestly (kirat karni), remember the Name (naam japna) and share (vand chhakna), and every gurdwara runs a langar, a free kitchen open to everyone.

fork.setup: the Provider has given your household its daily bread. in Sikh practice, what happens next?
options: keep it all; it was given to you.
share it: some goes on to others, as in the langar.
refuse it until you've earned more.
fork.reveal: earn, thank, share: the bread passes through Sikh hands and back out again, which is why every gurdwara has a free kitchen.

original.note: Gurmukhi: rozi, daily bread or livelihood, a Persian word; in Punjabi, rozi roti.

trapdoor: what you thought: the provider means God hands out food.
what it means: the One is the start of the chain of giving, and Sikhs pass the daily bread on through honest work and sharing.
what a scholar hears: rozi (Persian roz, day) and raazak (Arabic root r-z-q, to provide) place a Persianate epithet beside the Sikh triad of naam japna, kirat karni, vand chhakna.
recall: uncut hair, kept as part of the faith

chat.says: If God gives us our daily bread, why do we have to work so hard for it?
options: Sikhs earn honestly, thank the Giver and share; trusting never meant sitting and waiting.
Sikhs don't need to; the Provider sends food to whoever waits for it in faith.
Hard work is the real provider; thanking a Giver is just an old custom.
chat.meaning: Rozi, daily bread, comes from the One, and the Sikh pillars are honest work, remembering the Name and sharing, as in the langar.
